questions.q: Listed from most logical to most physical, what are the four layers of Oracle's storage hierarchy, per this lesson?
options: Tablespace, datafile, extent, block
Block, extent, datafile, tablespace
Datafile, tablespace, block, extent
Extent, block, tablespace, datafile
questions.explain: A tablespace is the logical unit, backed by one or more physical datafiles, which hold extents (contiguous groups of blocks), which hold blocks — the smallest I/O unit.

questions.q: What is the SYSTEM tablespace used for, per this lesson?
options: It holds the core data dictionary describing every object in the database
It stores temporary sort and hash join data
It exclusively holds undo data for rollback
It is an optional tablespace a DBA can choose not to create
questions.explain: SYSTEM holds the data dictionary — metadata about every object in the database — and is mandatory, not optional.

questions.q: What does the UNDO tablespace hold, and what is it used for?
options: The 'before' version of rows being changed, used for read consistency and rolling back uncommitted transactions
Cached parsed SQL statements and execution plans
Session-specific sort areas for each server process
The core data dictionary describing all database objects
questions.explain: UNDO data lets long-running queries see a consistent snapshot and lets uncommitted transactions be rolled back.

questions.q: Why is TEMP backed by a distinct file type (tempfiles) rather than regular datafiles, per this lesson?
options: TEMP handles sorts, hash joins, and other operations that spill to disk when they don't fit in memory — a different role from permanent data storage
TEMP is where the data dictionary is stored
TEMP is only used during database creation and never afterward
TEMP and SYSTEM are actually the same tablespace
questions.explain: TEMP tablespaces support transient operations like sorts and hash joins, and are backed by tempfiles as a distinct, non-permanent file type.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how safe is it to treat an Oracle tablespace as exactly equivalent to a SQL Server filegroup?
options: It's a reasonable starting intuition, but not a full equivalence — for example, SQL Server has no direct parallel to Oracle's UNDO tablespace
They are functionally identical in every respect
The comparison is completely wrong and should never be made
Filegroups and tablespaces are unrelated concepts with nothing in common
questions.explain: Both group physical files that objects get assigned to, which makes the analogy a useful starting point — but details like UNDO handling genuinely differ.
